opus-5.5.text:
Great question. When we think about which problems to put out to the academic community, there are a few criteria we keep coming back to.

First, the problem should matter for autonomous driving. We want challenges that reflect real bottlenecks we see in building the Waymo Driver, not toy problems. Things like 3D detection and tracking from lidar and camera, motion forecasting of other agents, and more recently closed-loop simulation and realistic agent behavior modeling. These are areas where progress translates fairly directly into a safer, more capable system.

Second, it has to be a problem the academic community can meaningfully attack. Some of our hardest challenges depend on enormous amounts of data, compute, or tight integration with our full stack, and those aren't great fits for a university lab. So we try to carve out well-defined, self-contained tasks with clear inputs and outputs, where a strong idea from a small team can genuinely move the needle.

Third, we care about having the right metrics. A lot of the value of a challenge comes from defining how you measure success. If the metric doesn't capture what matters on the road, people will optimize for the wrong thing. In motion forecasting, for example, we put real thought into handling multimodality and uncertainty, because the future is ambiguous and a single best guess isn't enough. For simulation agents, we wanted metrics that reward realistic distributions of behavior, not just matching a log.

Fourth, we like problems that are still open and where we think the field hasn't converged. If a benchmark is saturated, it's less interesting. We look for areas where new modeling paradigms, whether transformers, scaling, or generative approaches, could change the picture, and where we'd learn something from seeing many different ideas tried in parallel.

Finally, there's a data angle. The Waymo Open Dataset gives researchers access to diverse, high-quality real-world driving data at a scale that's otherwise hard to get. Pairing that data with carefully designed challenges lets the community push on problems that are both scientifically interesting and practically relevant. We get to see creative approaches we might not have thought of, and the community gets realistic problems to work on. That two-way exchange is really the point.

r001.rationale: The response says it favors open problems where the field has not converged and new modeling approaches could change the picture.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a planned camera-only end-to-end driving challenge or generalization to rare driving conditions.

r003.rationale: It mentions realistic simulation-agent behavior but does not describe generating traffic conditioned on a supplied road graph.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question we think about a lot, because we get one shot a year at this and we want the community's attention to go toward things that actually matter for the system we're building. There are a few criteria I'd point to.

The first is that the problem has to be genuinely important for autonomous driving and not just interesting in the abstract. So we look at where the real bottlenecks are. Perception is more mature than it was, so increasingly the harder questions are around behavior: predicting what other agents are going to do, especially in interactive situations, and then deciding what the autonomous vehicle itself should do. That's why we've leaned into motion prediction, interaction prediction, and more recently simulation and planning-style tasks, because those are the places where I think the field still has a lot of room to grow and where good ideas from academia can really move the needle.

The second criterion is that the problem has to be well-posed enough to benchmark. That sounds mundane, but it's actually quite hard. With detection you have a fairly clear metric. With behavior prediction you're dealing with multimodal futures, so you have to think carefully about what you're measuring. If you pick the wrong metric you end up with everyone optimizing for something that doesn't correlate with a safer or more capable driver. So a lot of our internal effort goes into defining the task and the metric, because the metric essentially shapes what the community spends its energy on.

The third is that the data has to support it. The reason we released the Waymo Open Dataset in the first place is that we have a scale and diversity of real-world driving data that most academic groups simply can't collect, with high-quality lidar and camera sensing across multiple cities and conditions. So we try to pose challenges that take advantage of that: long-horizon trajectories, dense interactions, unusual scenarios, the kind of long-tail situations that are rare in smaller datasets. If a problem can be solved just as well on a tiny dataset, it's probably not the best use of this resource.

And then finally, I'd say we want problems where the answers are transferable, where a method that does well on the challenge tells us something real about how to build the system. We're not trying to generate leaderboard chasing for its own sake. The best outcomes from past challenges have been when a new architecture or a new way of framing the problem comes out of the community, and we can learn from it and the whole field moves forward. That's really the goal: to get many more smart people thinking about the parts of the problem that we believe are the actual frontier.

r001.rationale: The response says challenge tasks should focus on areas with room to grow where academic ideas can move the needle, and values new approaches that advance the field.

r002.rationale: It mentions rare, long-tail driving scenarios as useful for challenges, but does not describe a planned camera-only end-to-end challenge or frame generalization to those conditions as its goal.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe generating realistic traffic conditioned on a supplied road graph.

astra-6.text:
We look for problems that are important for autonomous driving, but that also have a clear formulation and can be studied without access to an entire self-driving system. You want researchers to be able to take the data, understand the task, and measure whether their ideas are making progress.

Perception and motion prediction are good examples. What’s around the vehicle, how is it moving, and what might it do next? Prediction is particularly interesting because there isn’t necessarily one correct future. A pedestrian might cross the street or wait, and their decision can depend on what other road users do. How do you represent those possibilities and evaluate them meaningfully?

The goal is to make those kinds of research questions accessible, with data and evaluation methods that let the academic community contribute ideas that can ultimately matter for driving.

sol-6.1.text:
We look for problems that are important for autonomous driving, but that are also well defined enough that the academic community can make progress on them. Perception is a good example: detecting objects in three dimensions, tracking them over time, and understanding the scene around the vehicle. Another is motion prediction—given what you’ve observed, what might the other road users do next?

A useful challenge needs more than a large dataset. You need a clear task and an evaluation that measures something meaningful. We want researchers to be able to try an idea, compare it with other approaches, and understand where it helps and where it still fails. Ideally, these are problems that also raise broader research questions, so the work advances machine learning while helping us address real challenges in autonomous driving.
